claims.text: The enhanced corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a dense, uniform, Cr-rich passive oxide film.
A Cr-rich passive oxide film acts as a barrier against corrosive media.
The baseline steel has a uniform bulk microstructure and a naturally formed passive oxide film.
Adjusting oxygen partial pressure and temperature during pre-oxidation can systematically modify passive-film formation without changing bulk composition.
Temperatures near 320°C, 3.5 wt.% NaCl, and simulated reactor-water chemistries are representative service or test environments for the targeted applications.
Radiation effects are negligible over the proposed experimental timescale.
Passive-film density, uniformity, and Cr2O3 enrichment are the structural mediators of corrosion resistance.
A compact, defect-free passive oxide layer minimizes continuous metal dissolution.
Greater chromium enrichment of the passive film suppresses localized pitting.
Optimized pre-oxidation reduces overall corrosion rates compared with untreated steel having a naturally formed passive film.
Optimized pre-oxidation will increase polarization resistance relative to the baseline.
Optimized pre-oxidation will lower passive current density relative to the baseline.
Optimized pre-oxidation will increase pitting potential relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism holds broadly under moderate-to-high temperatures and aggressive chemical environments when bulk microstructure remains constant.
Underlying microstructural factors may independently contribute to passivation and corrosion resistance.
XPS and SEM can be used to compare passive-film composition and morphology across pre-oxidation conditions.
EIS, potentiodynamic polarization, and weight loss can measure corrosion performance across the treated and baseline samples.

The hypothesis is falsified if systematic differences in passive-film density or Cr enrichment produce no significant improvement in polarization resistance or pitting potential relative to the baseline.
